title: what my friends funeral taught me about money 2026 08 13
text:
NEW YORK, Aug 13 (Reuters) - As I was on vacation with my husband last week in Montana, I learned that one of my dearest friends in New York died just as our plane landed. She was only 58 and endured a terrible illness for nearly a decade, so I take comfort knowing that ​she is at peace.
Being far away, however, meant I could not get back in time for her funeral. Thankfully, I was able ‌to watch it on the livestream.
I mention this because her passing (along with another friend earlier this summer) has put a spotlight on end-of-life financial planning. Have you made preparations for your death and the death of your loved ones? Do you have money set aside to pay for it?
This is a kind reminder to make sure you have your important legal ​documents in place, which includes an updated will and healthcare directives along with beneficiaries assigned to brokerage, banking and other financial accounts. Please tell ​your loved ones know where to find these crucial documents. (I’ve added some more tips below.)
As always, I want to hear ⁠from you. If you have advice to share, write to me via the link in my bio.

In my latest installment of my “A$K Lauren” series, I tackle the thorny issue of when to refinance a mortgage.
Theoretically, you can refinance most mortgages at any time, but that doesn't mean borrowers should rush to the closing table, especially in the current interest-rate environment.
I spoke to five experts who say the real question isn't, "how soon," but, "does it ​make financial sense?"
Here are the key factors ​to consider before you refinance your ⁠mortgage.
Following up on my article 5 key legal documents every young American adult needs, Jim Tewalt, a certified financial planner and president at Estate Planning Solutions in Glendale, Arizona, sent an email with some more suggestions.
“While some states provide ​for informal probates or the transfer of property using forms such as a small estate affidavit to transfer property ​at death without going ⁠through the hassle of probate, there are four other ‘no-cost’ steps people with less-complicated estates can take,” Tewalt says.
POD designations. Adding a Payable on Death designation to a bank or credit union account assures transfer at death to a chosen beneficiary without probate.
TOD designations. Similar to a POD, a Transfer on Death designation is used for brokerage accounts to ⁠transfer stocks ​and other securities without the need to liquidate them first.
Beneficiary designations. Use these to transfer life insurance, ​retirement accounts such as IRA's (traditional and Roth) and 401(k)s to your chosen beneficiary.
Notarized list of gifts. A written, notarized statement of who you want to receive items of personal property such as fishing equipment, ​jewelry and other personal items.
